titleEn: Until I came into the sanctuaries of God
progression: | Am Am | F F | C G | Am Am |
intro: Twenty eight verses by Asaph, and the psalm that opens Book Three of the Psalter. It states its conclusion in the first line and then spends fifteen verses arguing against it: the wicked are comfortable, they die without pain, and the speaker who kept his hands clean is beaten every morning. The argument does not get answered by an argument. It gets answered by a place, in verse 17. For a learner the thing to track is one small word, the particle at {{1.2}}, which returns at {{13.0}} and {{18.0}}: three times someone says surely, and each time it introduces a different certainty, the last two contradicting the first.

stichs.en: A psalm of Asaph.
Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure of heart.

verses.summary: The verdict comes first, before any of the evidence. Read it again after verse 16 and it sounds like a man repeating something he was taught.

stichs.en: But as for me, my feet had almost turned aside,
my steps had all but been poured out from under me.

verses.summary: The crisis is described as a loss of footing, not a loss of belief. Nothing here is doubted yet; the ground is just gone.

stichs.en: For I envied the boastful,
when I kept seeing how well the wicked do.

verses.summary: The verb of seeing is imperfect, so it is not one glance but a habit of looking. Envy is named as the cause before the grievance is stated.

stichs.en: For they have no pangs at their death,
and their body is sound and fat.

verses.summary: The complaint starts at the end of a life rather than at the middle of it. Even dying costs them nothing, which is the part that stings.

stichs.en: They are not in the trouble that mortals have,
and they are not struck down along with everyone else.

verses.summary: Two words for a human being in one verse, both of them stressing weakness. The wicked are exempt from the category.

stichs.en: So pride is the chain around their throat,
and violence is the robe that wraps them.

verses.summary: Both images are clothing, and both are worn on purpose. What they did in private in verse 5 is now what they put on to be seen in.

stichs.en: Their eye bulges out of its fat,
the imaginings of the heart overflow.

verses.summary: Fat is prosperity made physical, and here it pushes the eye forward until the man cannot see past himself. The heart follows the eye.

stichs.en: They scoff, and they talk with malice,
they speak oppression from a great height.

verses.summary: The verb for speaking is used twice in six words. Their power is exercised through the mouth, which is what the next verse enlarges.

stichs.en: They have set their mouth against the heavens,
and their tongue struts about the earth.

verses.summary: Heaven and earth divided between one mouth and one tongue. The picture is of speech that has taken over the whole map.

stichs.en: So his people turn back here,
and waters of abundance are drained dry for them.

verses.summary: The hardest verse in the psalm and the one where translations part company. Something about a crowd going over to the winning side, and something about water.

stichs.en: And they say: how would God know?
Is there knowledge in the Most High?

verses.summary: The quotation is the centre of the indictment. They do not deny that God exists; they deny that God is informed.

stichs.en: Look at them: these are the wicked,
always at ease, and they keep piling up wealth.

verses.summary: The survey closes by pointing. Everything catalogued since verse 4 is gathered into one gesture and one balance sheet.

stichs.en: So I have kept my heart clean for nothing,
and washed my hands in innocence for nothing.

verses.summary: The second surely, and it cancels the first. Washed hands are priestly language, so the accusation is that the whole apparatus of purity paid nothing.

stichs.en: For I have been stricken all day long,
and my punishment arrives every morning.

verses.summary: The same root that verse 5 said never touches the wicked. He is inside the category they escape, and on a daily schedule.

stichs.en: If I had said: I will talk like that,
then I would have betrayed the generation of Your children.

verses.summary: The first word addressed to God, and it is about other people. What stops him is not that the complaint is false but that saying it aloud would break something.

stichs.en: And I thought hard, to understand this;
it was heavy labour in my eyes.

verses.summary: Thinking is tried and it fails. The word for the labour is the same word verse 5 used for the trouble the wicked never have.

stichs.en: until I came into the sanctuaries of God;
then I understood what their end would be.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm, and the answer is a location rather than a proof. The noun is plural, which readers have taken in more than one way.

stichs.en: Surely You set them on slippery ground,
You made them fall into ruins.

verses.summary: The third surely, and the grammar changes with it: from here on the psalm is addressed to God in the second person and never goes back.

stichs.en: How they became a desolation in an instant,
swept off, finished by terrors.

verses.summary: Four verbs of ending stacked with no conjunctions between the last two. The speed is the point: what took the psalm sixteen verses to envy takes one word to undo.

stichs.en: Like a dream once a man is awake, my Lord,
when You rouse Yourself You will despise their phantom.

verses.summary: The wicked are not destroyed here, they are reclassified: they were never solid enough to destroy. The word for their form is the one used for an image or a likeness.

stichs.en: When my heart was turning sour,
and I felt it pierce my kidneys,

verses.summary: The psalm goes back to the crisis in order to name it properly. The verb is the one used of dough going acid, and the kidneys are where the biblical body keeps its conscience.

stichs.en: I was a brute and I knew nothing,
I was a beast in Your presence.

verses.summary: The self-assessment is harsher than anything he said about the wicked. Note the last word: even as a beast he was with God, which is exactly what the next verse picks up.

stichs.en: Yet I am always with You;
You have taken hold of my right hand.

verses.summary: The same two words that ended verse 22 open this one, and the meaning flips. Being with God was the beast's condition and is now the man's security.

stichs.en: You guide me with Your counsel,
and afterward You will take me to glory.

verses.summary: Two words, afterward and glory, sitting next to each other with no preposition to say how they connect. That gap is where a great deal of later reading happens.

stichs.en: Whom do I have in heaven?
And with You beside me I want nothing on earth.

verses.summary: Heaven and earth again, the pair from verse 9, now emptied of everything except one presence. The mouth that filled both is not mentioned.

stichs.en: My flesh and my heart give out,
but the rock of my heart and my portion is God, forever.

verses.summary: The word heart appears twice in one line, once failing and once held up. Portion is land language: what the Levites were given instead of a field.

stichs.en: For look: those far from You will perish;
You put an end to everyone who strays from You.

glosses: You have put an end to
verses.summary: Distance is the only category left. The wicked of verse 3 are not defined by their wealth here but by how far away they stand.

stichs.en: But as for me, nearness to God is my good;
I have made the Lord GOD my refuge,
so that I can recount everything You do.

verses.summary: The word good comes back from verse 1, and the psalm ends by redefining it. Good is no longer an outcome that can be compared with someone else's; it is proximity.

pardes.body: One thesis, one long objection, one turn, one resolution. Verse 1 states the conclusion. Verses 2 to 16 dismantle it with a catalogue: the wicked die easily, dress in pride, speak against heaven, and get richer, while the man who kept himself clean is punished daily. Verse 17 is the turn, and what changes is not the evidence but the vantage point. From verse 18 the psalm speaks to God rather than about him, and it never returns to the third person. The last movement, verses 21 to 28, rereads the crisis: the speaker calls himself a beast, discovers that even the beast was being held by the hand, and ends by putting the word good from verse 1 back in place with a new meaning. Track the phrase but as for me at {{2.0}} and again at {{28.0}}. It opens the complaint and it closes the answer, and the two sentences it introduces are opposites.

This psalm carries an unusual number of cruxes, and a learner should know which are real. In verse 1 the consonants of the word for to Israel can be divided differently to give to the upright, which yields God is good to the upright rather than to Israel. That division is a conjecture; the received text and the vocalisation both read Israel, and the reading is disputed. Verse 4 has the same kind of problem: {{4.3}}, at their death, can be re-divided to attach its last syllable to the following clause, giving they have no pangs, sound and fat is their body. Verse 10 is genuinely obscure, and published translations differ from each other more than they differ from the Hebrew. At {{20.3}} the consonants are read by some as in the city and by others as when You rouse Yourself, from the root for waking, which is the reading the dream in the same verse supports. In verse 22 the word for beast is a plural form used for a single animal, which is why some render it a great brute. The verb at {{24.4}} is the ordinary verb to take, and it is also the verb used of Enoch in Genesis 5 and of Elijah in 2 Kings 2, which is why the line has been read as more than a promise of guidance.

Psalm 73 opens Book Three of the Psalter and heads the block of Asaph psalms, so its placement puts a crisis of theodicy where a reader expects a hymn. Later readers took the plural at {{17.3}}, the sanctuaries, to mean more than a building, and the word for their end in the same verse carries in later Hebrew the sense of what comes after, so that the answer given in the sanctuary is understood as a view past the edge of a lifetime. On that reading verses 24 to 26 are not about consolation in old age but about what survives it, and the flesh failing in verse 26 is allowed to fail. There is a quieter reading that stays inside this life: what the sanctuary supplies is not information about the future but company in the present, and the proof is verse 23, where the hand was already being held during the years the speaker calls himself a beast. Both readings are current. Verse 15 is the ethical hinge of the whole thing: the speaker does not conclude that his complaint was wrong, only that broadcasting it would have injured people who had done nothing, and that judgement is made before he has any answer at all.

Read inwardly, the psalm is about the two things a person can take as a measure. The wicked are measured from outside, by fat, clothing, wealth and the absence of pain, and the mystical reading takes the eye pushed forward by fat in verse 7 as the exact image of a consciousness that can no longer see anything but its own surface. Against that, verse 26 sets an inner measure and calls it the rock of my heart, a phrase in which the heart has a foundation that is not the heart. The beast of verse 22 is read as the animal soul, the part of a person that is entirely honest about wanting what the wicked have, and the psalm does not kill it; it discovers that it too was being held by the right hand, which is the side of kindness. The last word of the whole argument is nearness, at {{28.1}}, a noun built from the verb to draw close: not a reward for the pure of heart, but the definition of what good was in verse 1 all along.
